avengement: The inflicting of retributive punishment; satisfaction taken. Milton.
avena: A genus of grasses, including the common oat (Avena sativa); the oat grasses.
aventine: Pertaining to Mons Aventinus, one of the seven hills on which Rome stood. Bryant. | A post of security or defense. (poetic) Into the castle's tower, The only Aventine that now is left him. Beau. & Fl.
averroist: One of a sect of peripatetic philosophers, who appeared in Italy before the restoration of learning; so denominated from Averroes, or Averrhoes, a celebrated Arabian philosopher. He held the doctrine of monopsychism.
aviseful: Watchful; circumspect. (old) With sharp, aviseful eye. Spenser.
averruncate: 1. To avert; to ward off. (old) Hudibras. 2. To root up. (old) Johnson.
avoirdupois: 1. Goods sold by weight. (old) 2. Avoirdupois weight. 3. Weight; heaviness; as, a woman of much avoirdupois. [Colloq.] Avoirdupois weight, a system of weights by which coarser commodities are weighed, such as hay, grain, butter, sugar, tea.
avoyer: A chief magistrate of a free imperial city or canton of Switzerland. (old)
avoset: A grallatorial bird, of the genus Recurvirostra; the scooper. The bill is long and bend upward toward the tip. The American species is R. Americana. [Written also avocette.]
avoidance: 1. The act of annulling; annulment. 2. The act of becoming vacant, or the state of being vacant; -- specifically used for the state of a benefice becoming void by the death, deprivation, or resignation of the incumbent. Wolsey, . . . on every avoidance of St. Peter's chair, was sitting down therein, when suddenly some one or other clapped in before him. Fuller. 3.
average: 1. (OLd Eng. Law) That service which a tenant owed his lord, to be done by the work beasts of the tenant, as the carriage of wheat, turf, etc. 2. Etym: [Cf. F. avarie damage to ship or cargo.] (Com.)… | 1. Pertaining to an average or mean; medial; containing a mean proportion; of a mean size, quality, ability, etc.; ordinary; usual; as, an average rate of profit; an average amount of rain;
avoider: 1. The person who carries anything away, or the vessel in which things are carried away. Johnson. 2. One who avoids, shuns, or escapes.
avaunt: Begone; depart; -- a word of contempt or abhorrence, equivalent to the phrase "Get thee gone." | 1. To advance; to move forward; to elevate. (old) Spenser. 2. To depart; to move away. (old) Coverdale.
availably: In an available manner; profitably; advantageously; efficaciously.
aviator: (a) An experimenter in aviation. (b) A flying machine.
avoid: 1. To empty. (old) Wyclif. 2. To emit or throw out; to void; as, to avoid excretions. (old) Sir T. Browne. 3. To quit or evacuate; to withdraw from. (old) Six of us only stayed, and the rest avoided… | 1. To retire; to withdraw. (old) David avoided out of his presence. 1 Sam. xviii. 11. 2. (Law) To become void or vacant. (old) Ayliffe.
avatar: 1. (Hindoo Myth.) The descent of a deity to earth, and his incarnation as a man or an animal; -- chiefly associated with the incarnations of Vishnu. 2. Incarnation; manifestation as an object of worship or admiration.
avenue: 1. A way or opening for entrance into a place; a passage by which a place may by reached; a way of approach or of exit. "The avenues leading to the city by land." Macaulay. On every side were expanding new avenues of inquiry. Milman. 2. The principal walk or approach to a house which is withdrawn from the road, especially, such approach bordered on each side by trees;
aviado: One who works a mine with means provided by another. [Sp. Amer. & Southwestern U. S.]
avocado: The pulpy fruit of Persea gratissima, a tree of tropical America. It is about the size and shape of a large pear; -- called also avocado pear, alligator pear, midshipman's butter.
averruncator: An instrument for pruning trees, consisting of two blades, or a blade and a hook, fixed on the end of a long rod.
avemary: 1. A salutation and prayer to the Virgin Mary, as mother of God; -- used in the Roman Catholic church. To number Ave Maries on his beads. Shak. 2. A particular time (as in Italy, at the ringing of the bells about half an hour after sunset, and also at early dawn), when the people repeat the Ave Maria. Ave Maria ! blessed be the hour ! Byron.
aventre: To thrust forward (at a venture), as a spear. (old) Spenser.
avenious: Being without veins or nerves, as the leaves of certain plants.
aversely: 1. Backward; in a backward direction; as, emitted aversely. 2. With repugnance or aversion; unwillingly.
avenalin: A crystalline globulin, contained in oat kernels, very similar in composition to excelsin, but different in reactions and crystalline form.
avifauna: The birds, or all the kinds of birds, inhabiting a region.
avernian: Of or pertaining to Avernus, a lake of Campania, in Italy, famous for its poisonous vapors, which ancient writers fancied were so malignant as to kill birds flying over it. It was represented by the poets to be connected with the infernal regions.
avocation: 1. A calling away; a diversion. [Obs. or Archaic] Impulses to duty, and powerful avocations from sin. South. 2. That which calls one away from one's regular employment or vocation. Heaven is his vocation, and therefore he counts earthly employments avocations. Fuller.
avowance: 1. Act of avowing; avowal. 2. Upholding; defense; vindication. (old) Can my avowance of king-murdering be collected from anything here written by me Fuller.
averpenny: Money paid by a tenant in lieu of the service of average.
avenge: 1. To take vengeance for; to exact satisfaction for by punishing the injuring party; to vindicate by inflicting pain or evil on a wrongdoer. He will avenge the blood of his servants. Deut. xxxii. 43. | To take vengeance. Levit. xix. 18.
avulsion: 1. A tearing asunder; a forcible separation. The avulsion of two polished superficies. Locke. 2. A fragment torn off. J. Barlow. 3. (Law) The sudden removal of lands or soil from the estate of one man to that of another by an inundation or a current, or by a sudden change in the course of a river by which a part of the estate of one man is cut off and joined to the estate of…
avener: An officer of the king's stables whose duty it was to provide oats for the horses. (old)
available: 1. Having sufficient power, force, or efficacy, for the object; effectual; valid; as, an available plea. (old) Laws human are available by consent. Hooker. 2. Such as one may avail one's self of; capable of being used for the accomplishment of a purpose; usable; profitable; advantageous; convertible into a resource; as, an available measure; an available candidate.
aviette: A heavier-than-air flying machine in which the motive power is furnished solely by the aviator.
avolate: To fly away; to escape; to exhale. (old)
aver: A work horse, or working ox. [Obs. or Dial. Eng.] | 1. To assert, or prove, the truth of. (old) 2. (Law) To avouch or verify; to offer to verify; to prove or justify. See Averment. 3. To affirm with confidence; to declare in a positive manner, as in…
avercorn: A reserved rent in corn, formerly paid to religious houses by their tenants or farmers. Kennet.
avaricious: Actuated by avarice; greedy of gain; immoderately desirous of accumulating property. Syn. -- Greedy; stingy; rapacious; griping; sordid; close. -- Avaricious, Covetous, Parsimonious, Penurious, Miserly, Niggardly. The avaricious eagerly grasp after it at the expense of others, though not of necessity with a design to save, since a man may be covetous and yet a spendthrift.
avel: To pull away. (old) Yet are not these parts avelled. Sir T. Browne.
avidity: Greediness; strong appetite; eagerness; intenseness of desire; as, to eat with avidity. His books were received and read with avidity. Milward.
avantcourier: A person dispatched before another person or company, to give notice of his or their approach.
avocet: A grallatorial bird, of the genus Recurvirostra; the scooper. The bill is long and bend upward toward the tip. The American species is R. Americana. [Written also avocette.]
aventure: 1. Accident; chance; adventure. (old) Chaucer. 2. (Old Law) A mischance causing a person's death without felony, as by drowning, or falling into the fire.
aviate: To fly, or navigate the air, in an aëroplane or heavier-than- air flying machine. [Colloq.]
availability: 1. The quality of being available; availableness. Note: The word is sometimes used derogatively in the sense of "mere availableness," or capability of success without regard to worthiness. He was . . . nominated for his availability. Lowell. 2. That which is available.
avoke: To call from or back again. (old) Bp. Burnet.
avellane: In the form of four unhusked filberts; as, an avellane cross.
avowee: The person who has a right to present to a benefice; the patron; an advowee. See Advowson.
avile: To abase or debase; to vilify; to depreciate. (old) Want makes us know the price of what we avile. B. Jonson.
avise: 1. To look at; to view; to think of. (old) Chaucer. 2. To advise; to counsel. (old) Shak. To avise one's self, to consider with one's self, to reflect, to deliberate. (old) Chaucer. | To consider; to reflect. (old)
avant: The front of an army. (old) See Van.
avowed: Openly acknowledged or declared; admitted. -- A*vow"ed*ly (, adv.
avestan: Of or pertaining to the Avesta or the language of the Avesta. - -n. The language of the Avesta; -- less properly called Zend.
aviso: 1. Information; advice. 2. An advice boat, or dispatch boat.
averruncation: 1. The act of averting. (old) 2. Eradication. De Quincey.
avemaria: 1. A salutation and prayer to the Virgin Mary, as mother of God; -- used in the Roman Catholic church. To number Ave Maries on his beads. Shak. 2. A particular time (as in Italy, at the ringing of the bells about half an hour after sunset, and also at early dawn), when the people repeat the Ave Maria. Ave Maria ! blessed be the hour ! Byron.
avert: To turn aside, or away; as, to avert the eyes from an object; to ward off, or prevent, the occurrence or effects of; as, how can the danger be averted "To avert his ire." Milton. | To turn away. (old) Cold and averting from our neighbor's good. Thomson.
avulse: To pluck or pull off. Shenstone.
averse: 1. Turned away or backward. (old) The tracks averse a lying notice gave, And led the searcher backward from the cave. Dryden. 2. Having a repugnance or opposition of mind; disliking; disinclined; | To turn away. (old) B. Jonson.
avale: 1. To cause to descend; to lower; to let fall; to doff. (old) Chaucer. 2. To bring low; to abase. (old) Sir H. Wotton. 3. (v. i.) To descend; to fall; to dismount. (old) And from their sweaty courses did avale. Spenser.
aversation: A turning from with dislike; aversion. [Obs.or Archaic] Some men have a natural aversation to some vices or virtues, and a natural affection to others. Jer. Taylor.
aviation: The art or science of flying.
avantguard: The van or advanced body of an army. See Vanguard.
availableness: 1. Competent power; validity; efficacy; as, the availableness of a title. (old) 2. Quality of being available; capability of being used for the purpose intended. Sir M. Hale.
avid: Longing eagerly for; eager; greedy. "Avid of gold, yet greedier of renown." Southey.
avocative: That which calls aside; a dissuasive.
avolation: The act of flying; flight; evaporation. (old)
avarice: 1. An excessive or inordinate desire of gain; greediness after wealth; covetousness; cupidity. To desire money for its own sake, and in order to hoard it up, is avarice. Beattie. 2. An inordinate desire for some supposed good. All are taught an avarice of praise. Goldsmith.
avoidable: 1. Capable of being vacated; liable to be annulled or made invalid; voidable. The charters were not avoidable for the king's nonage. Hale. 2. Capable of being avoided, shunned, or escaped.
avow: 1. To declare openly, as something believed to be right; to own or acknowledge frankly; as, a man avows his principles or his crimes. Which I to be the of Israel's God Avow, and challenge Dagon to… | To bind, or to devote, by a vow. (old) Wyclif.
avowry: 1. An advocate; a patron; a patron saint. (old) Let God alone be our avowry. Latimer. 2. The act of the distrainer of goods, who, in an action of replevin, avows and justifies the taking in his own right. Blackstone.
avicular: Of or pertaining to a bird or to birds.
avowable: Capable of being avowed, or openly acknowledged, with confidence. Donne.
avouchment: The act of avouching; positive declaration. (old) Milton.
avuncular: Of or pertaining to an uncle. In these rare instances, the law of pedigree, whether direct or avuncular, gives way. I. Taylor.
averted: Turned away, esp. as an expression of feeling; also, offended; unpropitious. Who scornful pass it with averted eye. Keble.
aventail: The movable front to a helmet; the ventail.
avenger: 1. One who avenges or vindicates; as, an avenger of blood. 2. One who takes vengeance. (old) Milton.
avouch: 1. To appeal to; to cite or claim as authority. (old) They avouch many successions of authorities. Coke. 2. To maintain a just or true; to vouch for. We might be disposed to question its authencity,… | Evidence; declaration. (old) The sensible and true avouch Of mine own eyes. Shak.
avignonberry: The fruit of the Rhamnus infectorius, eand of other species of the same genus; -- so called from the city of Avignon, in France. It is used by dyers and painters for coloring yellow. Called also French berry.
avens: A plant of the genus Geum, esp. Geum urbanum, or herb bennet.
avowal: An open declaration; frank acknowledgment; as, an avowal of such principles. Hume.
avalanche: 1. A large mass or body of snow and ice sliding swiftly down a mountain side, or falling down a precipice. 2. A fall of earth, rocks, etc., similar to that of an avalanche of snow or ice. 3. A sudden, great, or irresistible descent or influx of anything.
averter: One who, or that which, averts.
avernal: Of or pertaining to Avernus, a lake of Campania, in Italy, famous for its poisonous vapors, which ancient writers fancied were so malignant as to kill birds flying over it. It was represented by the poets to be connected with the infernal regions.
aviary: A house, inclosure, large cage, or other place, for keeping birds confined; a bird house. Lincolnshire may be termed the aviary of England. Fuller.
avenage: A quantity of oats paid by a tenant to a landlord in lieu of rent. Jacob.
aventurine: 1. A kind of glass, containing gold-colored spangles. It was produced in the first place by the accidental (par aventure) dropping of some brass filings into a pot of melted glass. 2. (Min.) A variety of translucent quartz, spangled throughout with scales of yellow mica.
ave: 1. An ave Maria. He repeated Aves and Credos. Macaulay. 2. A reverential salutation. Their loud applause and aves vehement. Shak.
avowant: The defendant in replevin, who avows the distress of the goods, and justifies the taking. Cowell.
avicularia: See prehensile processes on the cells of some Bryozoa, often having the shape of a bird's bill.
avicula: A genus of marine bivalves, having a pearly interior, allied to the pearl oyster; -- so called from a supposed resemblance of the typical species to a bird.
avocate: To call off or away; to withdraw; to transfer to another tribunal. [Obs. or Archaic] One who avocateth his mind from other occupations. Barrow. He, at last, . . . avocated the cause to Rome. Robertson.
averseness: The quality of being averse; opposition of mind; unwillingness.
aves: The class of Vertebrata that includes the birds. Note: Aves, or birds, have a complete double circulation, oviparous, reproduction, front limbs peculiarly modified as wings; and they bear feathers. All existing birds have a horny beak, without teeth; but some Mesozoic fossil birds (Odontornithes) had conical teeth inserted in both jaws.
aversion: 1. A turning away. (old) Adhesion to vice and aversion from goodness. Bp. Atterbury. 2. Opposition or repugnance of mind; fixed dislike; antipathy; disinclination; reluctance. Mutual aversion of races. Prescott. His rapacity had made him an object of general aversion. Macaulay. Note: It is now generally followed by to before the object.
avail: 1. To turn to the advantage of; to be of service to; to profit; to benefit; to help; as, artifices will not avail the sinner in the day of judgment. O, what avails me now that honor high ! Milton. 2. | To be of use or advantage; to answer the purpose; to have strength, force, or efficacy sufficient to accomplish the object; as, the plea in bar must avail, that is, be sufficient to defeat the suit;
avenaceous: Belonging to, or resembling, oats or the oat grasses.
averment: 1. The act of averring, or that which is averred; affirmation; positive assertion. Signally has this averment received illustration in the course of recent events. I. Taylor. 2. Verification; establishment by evidence. Bacon. 3. (Law) A positive statement of facts; an allegation; an offer to justify or prove what is alleged.
